Professor '''Bruce Harold John McKellar''' {{post-nominals|country=AUS|AC}} (born 1941) is an Australian theoretical particle physicist who is Honorary [[Professorial Fellow]] at the Centre of Excellence for Particle Physics at the Terascale (CoEPP)<ref>[http://www.coepp.org.au/ Centre of Excellence for Particle Physics at the Terascale (CoEPP)], www.coepp.org.au</ref> in the School of Physics at [[The University of Melbourne]]. The [[International Union of Pure and Applied Physics]] (IUPAP) elected him as its President-Designate in 2012.  In November 2014, McKellar became President of IUPAP, the first-ever Australian to take on this role.<ref>{{cite news |publisher= Australian Academy of Science |title=Australian physicist and Fellow to lead International Physics Union |url=https://www.science.org.au/news/australian-physicist-and-fellow-lead-international-physics-union }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=McKellar |first=Bruce H. J. |date=2017-10-01 |title=Commentary: International Union of Pure and Applied Physics and you |url=https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/article/70/10/10/910373/Commentary-International-Union-of-Pure-and-Applied |journal=Physics Today |language=en |volume=70 |issue=10 |pages=10–11 |doi=10.1063/PT.3.3707 |bibcode=2017PhT....70j..10M |issn=0031-9228|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

McKellar is a theoretical particle physicist who is known for his work on [[particle physics]] and many other fields such as [[nuclear physics]] and [[cosmology]]. His other work has had applications in [[photography]], atmospheric physics and [[geophysics]], as well as implications for [[pure mathematics]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Australian physicist to lead international physics union |url=http://www.coepp.org.au/australian-physicist-lead-international-physics-union |publisher=www.coepp.org.au |date=17 Nov 2014 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150331005741/http://www.coepp.org.au/australian-physicist-lead-international-physics-union |archivedate=2015-03-31 }}</ref>

On [[Australia Day]] ([[2014 Australia Day Honours|26 January 2014]]), McKellar was appointed a [[Companion of the Order of Australia]] (AC) by Governor-General [[Quentin Bryce]], for his service to science, particularly [[theoretical physics]], as an academic, educator and researcher, through seminal contributions to scientific development organisations, and as an author and mentor.<ref name=ACCitation>{{cite web |title=Citations - Companions of the Order of Australia |url=https://www.gg.gov.au/sites/default/files/files/honours/ad/Media%20Notes%20-%20AC%20%28final%29.pdf |date= 26 January 2014}}</ref> The AC is Australia's highest civilian honour.

==Early years and education==
McKellar grew up in [[Bedgerabong]] in NSW, attending Bedgerabong Primary School,<ref>[http://www.bedgerebon-p.schools.nsw.edu.au/ Bedgerabong Primary School], www.bedgerebon-p.schools.nsw.edu.au</ref> which was then a one-teacher school.  His father was the teacher. He then attended Forbes High School<ref>[http://www.forbes-h.schools.nsw.edu.au/ Forbes High School], www.forbes-h.schools.nsw.edu.au</ref> before moving to Sydney at 16 to study a Bachelor of Science at the [[University of Sydney]], which he completed with First Class Honours and the University Medal for Physics.

He received his PhD from the [[University of Sydney]] in 1965,<ref>{{cite web|title=Faculty of Science at the University of Melbourne Biographical entry |url=http://www.austehc.unimelb.edu.au/umfs/biogs/UMFS150b.htm}}</ref> and a Doctor of Science from [[the University of Melbourne]] in 1976.

==Academic career==
Immediately on completion of his PhD, McKellar was appointed as a lecturer at the [[University of Sydney]]. In 1965, McKellar was invited by [[J. Robert Oppenheimer]] to become a member of the [[Institute for Advanced Study|Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton, USA]], which he undertook from 1966 to 1968.<ref name=sciencearchive>{{cite web |title=Science Archive entry |url=http://www.sciencearchive.org.au/events/sats/sats2009/ecr_awards_mckellar.html |access-date=2015-05-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518071600/http://www.sciencearchive.org.au/events/sats/sats2009/ecr_awards_mckellar.html |archive-date=2015-05-18 |url-status=dead }}</ref>  He then returned to the [[University of Sydney]]. In 1972, at the age of 30, McKellar was appointed as the Professor of [[Theoretical Physics]] at [[Melbourne University]]. He retired from this role in 2007.<ref name=sciencearchive/>

He has held visiting positions at the [[French Atomic Energy Commission]], Saclay (France), the [[TRIUMF]] Laboratories (Canada), the [[University of Washington]] ([[Seattle]] United States), the [[Los Alamos Laboratory]] (United States), [[CERN]] (Switzerland), the [[Yukawa Institute]] (Japan), the [[National Taiwan University]], the [[National University of Singapore]], the [[Australian National University]] and the [[University of Adelaide]].

At [[Princeton University|Princeton]], McKellar began his work on weak interactions, calculating the parity violation expected in [[Atomic nucleus|nuclei]].  He also started his work on three and many body nuclear forces. It was characteristic of this work that he was applying the current [[algebra]] techniques of particle physics to obtain results about [[Atomic nucleus|nuclei]]. During his time at the [[University of Melbourne]], McKellar and his collaborators published their definitive study on three-nucleon forces, famously known as the "Tucson-Melbourne" force.<ref>[http://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/9789812770301_0001 Tucson-Melbourne force], www.worldscientific.com</ref>  His work on weak interactions led to the calculation of the electric dipole moments expected for the nucleon and atoms in various models of these interactions.  This work then evolved into studies of related effects in the B meson system.

McKellar and his students also did foundational work on the behaviour of neutrinos propagating through a dense background of neutrinos as one finds in the early universe. He is well known for the "He McKellar Wilkens" phase, a seminal quantum physics result predicted by He and McKellar<ref>[http://journals.aps.org/pra/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevA.47.3424#references He and McKellar]</ref> and Wilkens (independently)<ref>[http://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.72.5 Wilkens]</ref> in 1993–94.

McKellar has made a significant contribution to the development of the study of physics in Australia.  He was elected a [[Fellow of the Australian Academy of Science]] in 1987, was its Vice President for Physical Sciences from 2000–2004 and its Foreign Secretary from 2004–2006.<ref name=ACCitation/> He was a founding member of the [[Australian Research Council]], playing a key role in both its establishment and development.<ref name=ACCitation/>

McKellar actively facilitates physics research, policy development and international collaboration globally, especially in the [[Asia-Pacific]] Region. He served on the board of trustees of the SIA Pacific Centre for Theoretical Physics<ref>[https://www.apctp.org/main/ Asia Pacific Centre for Theoretical Physics]</ref> and on the Council of the Association of Asia Pacific Physical Societies<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.aapps.org/main/ |title=Association of Asia Pacific Physical Societies |access-date=12 May 2015 |archive-date=24 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201024022331/http://www.aapps.org/main/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> for many years.<ref name=ACCitation/> He chaired the Regional Committee for Asia and the Pacific<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.icsu.org/asia-pacific/about-icsu-roap/structure/regional-committee/?icsudocid=past-members |title=Regional Committee for Asia and the Pacific |access-date=2015-05-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518085241/http://www.icsu.org/asia-pacific/about-icsu-roap/structure/regional-committee/?icsudocid=past-members |archive-date=2015-05-18 |url-status=dead }}</ref> of the [[International Council for Science]] (ICSU) (2009–2011), as well as the Australia and New Zealand Association for the Advancement of Science (ANZAAS)<ref>[http://www.anzaas.org.au/ Australia and New Zealand Association for the Advancement of Science]</ref> (1992–1998).<ref name=ACCitation/>

McKellar is a Fellow of the [[Australian Institute of Physics]], the [[Institute of Physics]] (UK), the [[American Physical Society]], and the [[Australian Academy of Science]].<ref name=ACCitation/>

==Awards and honours==
*2014: [[Companion of the Order of Australia]]<ref name=AC>{{cite web |url= https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/1148817 |title= Companion of the Order of Australia |date= 26 January 2014 |publisher= It's an Honour }} "For eminent service to science, particularly the study of theoretical physics, as an academic, educator and researcher, through seminal contributions to scientific development organisations, and as an author and mentor."</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=IOP Institute of Physics entry |url=http://www.iop.org/news/14/feb/page_62440.html}}</ref>
*2009: [[Matthew Flinders Medal and Lecture]], [[Australian Academy of Science]]
*2006: [[Harrie Massey Medal and Prize]], [[Institute of Physics]] (UK) and the [[Australian Institute of Physics]]
*2001: [[Centenary Medal]]<ref name=CM>{{cite web |url= https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/1126373 |title= Centenary Medal |date= 1 January 2001 |publisher= It's an Honour }} "For service to Australian society and science in theoretical physics"</ref>
*1992: [[Walter Boas Medal]], [[Australian Institute of Physics]]
*1991: [[Thomas Ranken Lyle Medal]], [[Australian Academy of Science]]
*1987: [[Fellow of the Australian Academy of Science]]
*1977: Research Medal, [[Royal Society of Victoria]]
*1973: [[Pawsey Medal]], [[Australian Academy of Science]]
*1962: University Medal, [[University of Sydney]]

==Personal life==
Bruce McKellar married Loris Huckel in 1963. They have 2 children and 4 grandchildren and live in Melbourne, Australia.
